title: T Cell Memory to Viruses
text:
A better understanding of the mechanisms that regulate CD8 T cell responses during chronic viral infection is
required to improve immunotherapies that will increase T cell function and reduce viral load. Our studies will
provide the fundamental basis for developing rational approaches for immunotherapy of chronic viral infections.

title: T cell migration and cardiovascular toxicity in immunotherapy
text:
CAR-T cell immunotherapy has emerged as a promising therapeutic option with complete and durable responses
in several cancer types. However, CAR-T cell therapies have largely failed in patients with solid tumors. We will
investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms that regulate CAR-T cell migration to target solid tumors. The
effectiveness of clinical approaches using T cells will be enhanced by our discovery of important mediators that
can improve the tissue-specific migration of adoptively transferred therapeutic T cells while minimizing
sequestration at nonspecific tissue sites.

title: Investigating the Molecular Effects of Social Deprivation on Neuroblastoma Tumorigenesis and Progression
text:
Neuroblastoma is a life-threatening childhood cancer, and outcomes remain poor for children
with high-risk disease. This project investigates how sustained stress signaling influences tumor
growth and response to therapy by altering neuroendocrine, immune, and metabolic pathways.
By identifying targetable biological mechanisms, this research will inform new therapeutic
strategies to improve outcomes for children with neuroblastoma.

title: Auditory-based navigation: attentional shifts rapidly modulate hippocampal codes
text:
Hippocampal dysfunctions, which arise in the course of aging, mental illnesses (major depression,
schizophrenia), neurological disorders (epilepsy) or neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s),
can lead to impairment of navigation and spatial attention. Little is known about the link between spatial attention
and hippocampal spatial codes, primarily because it is difficult to track moment-to-moment changes in attention
in traditional research animals. The proposed experiments will bridge this gap by using novel technologies and
new experimental paradigms in echolocating bats, which enable measurement of attentional shifts on a rapid
timescale, to elucidate how spatial attention modulates hippocampal spatial codes—a key open question in the
neurobiology of navigation.

title: Targeting a Novel Pocket on ITGAV
text:
The proposed research aims to fill an unmet clinical need in treating aggressive cancers such as colon,
pancreatic, and breast. We found that Integrin Alpha V (ITGAV) is necessary for the survival of these cancers
and that a novel pocket on its structure can be targeted with a drug. Additionally, we will investigate the complex
signaling controlled by ITGAV to propose combinational therapies and create new therapeutic strategies to treat
these cancers.

title: Cancer Prevention & Population Sciences Program
text: CANCER PREVENTION AND POPULATION SCIENCES (CPPS) PROGRAM PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The mission of the Cancer Prevention and Population Sciences (CPPS) Program is to conduct exceptional translational research in cancer prevention and control. CPPS achieves this goal by promoting and facilitating innovative, transdisciplinary scientific interactions focused on reducing cancer incidence, morbidity, and mortality. CPPS research focuses on meeting the cancer prevention and control needs of the populations in our catchment area. The Program is led by Drs. Hoda Badr and Philip Lupo, internationally recognized experts in cancer survivorship and genetic epidemiology. CPPS has 41 Research and 13 Clinical Members. Our research portfolio (annual direct) totals $24.1 million, of which $11.6 million is from NCI. During the current funding period, CPPS members published 689 papers, of which 36% were intra-programmatic and 26% inter-programmatic. Approximately 24% were published in journals with an impact factor above 10. Following the last CCSG review and exceptional targeted recruitments, CPPS leadership conducted an extensive strategic planning initiative that re-focused our programmatic research efforts to reflect two themes. Theme 1 (Cancer Etiology and Primary Prevention) includes research on the genetic and environmental causes of pre-malignant and malignant conditions across the lifespan, gene-environment interactions, and primary prevention. This theme also leverages advanced analytics to refine risk assessments, thereby advancing precision medicine by enabling more personalized approaches to cancer prevention. Theme 2 (Secondary Prevention and Cancer Outcomes) focuses on screening and early detection, understanding mechanisms of cancer outcomes, and conducting interventional and observational research to enhance survivorship, cancer care, and outcomes. Overall cancer health, including addressing social determinants of health, is a major emphasis of our Program, underscored by the methodological expertise of our members, which spans a broad spectrum of approaches from data analytics to participatory research methods. This unique blend of expertise both promotes inter- and intra-programmatic collaborations and strengthens integration of our Program themes. Our collaboration with COE has been crucial in establishing bidirectional research-community partnerships to make our research more relevant and impactful by ensuring it is informed by and directly benefits the communities we serve. Together with CRTEC, we have substantially broadened our efforts to train the next generation of cancer prevention and control researchers across the career continuum. In sum, CPPS conducts innovative, translational research that is bolstered by strong funding, productive collaborations, and scholarly output and reflects DLDCCC’s unwavering commitment to cancer care for the community we serve and beyond.

title: Genetic Variation in AMD Progression  and Treatment Response
text:
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss. This project aims to improve
predictions of AMD progression and treatment outcomes through machine learning-based OCT analysis and
subgroup analysis to identify critical biomarkers and address disease heterogeneity. Integrating these
approaches with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) will uncover genetic loci and refine polygenic risk
scores (PRS), enabling personalized AMD management.

title: Serotonin and Prefrontal Somatostatin Interneuron Regulation of Impulsivity and Cognitive Flexibility
text:
Inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility are often disrupted in psychiatric disorders. This project aims to
understand how serotonin, a key chemical messenger, interacts with inhibitory neurons that help regulate
these behaviors. By studying how these neurons respond to serotonin during behavior, we hope to identify new
targets for treating symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric disorders.

title: Targeting AVIL, a novel oncogene in rhabdomyosarcoma
text:
Despite collaborative national trials of multimodal therapy and chemotherapy intensification, the outcome for
patients with advanced stage rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) has not improved in two decades. We have identified
a cancer-driving factor, to which RMS cells are addicted. In this application, we propose the systematic
investigation of targeting this factor as a novel approach against RMS.

title: Core C: Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core
text: PROJECT ABSTRACT – BIOSTATISTICS AND BIOINFORMATICS CORE The Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core will assist with study design, data management, analysis, and manuscript preparation for the individual projects as well as the other Cores of the Cancer Health Disparities SPORE in Endometrial Cancer. The core will be staffed by two directors with varied analytic expertise as well as a team of specialized statisticians, bioinformaticians, and a data manager to provide an array of analytic knowledge and expertise to the SPORE projects. The computational and data management services provided by the core will expand upon the resources already available to the Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center Bioinformatics Shared Resource. This will include the use of a high-performance computer cluster, dedicated storage, standardized data processing workflows, sample tracking, as well as database design, implementation, documentation, maintenance, and user support. The core will provide statistical and analytic support that will cover power analysis along with the use of field-standard and cutting-edge regression and machine learning approaches for cross-platform and multi-domain data integration to facilitate understanding the inter-relationship between social factors, clinical factors, and endometrial cancer biology. For all analyses, biostatisticians and bioinformaticians from the core will work together to develop, review, and approve analysis plans, assign appropriate personnel for each analysis task, discuss and solve analytical and technical challenges, review analysis code and report, and write manuscripts.

title: Translational regulation of PGC1alpha and oxidative metabolism
text:
Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders represent a major threat to the American health, as well as a
substantial economic burden. Thermogenic fat is a specialized tissue whose role is to expend excess energy,
and activating this tissue might ameliorate metabolic disease in humans. This proposal aims to understand
how this cell type is naturally regulated in order to identify new ways to therapeutically activate it.

title: Kinase Multitargeting for Glaucoma Neuroprotection
text:
We previously identified dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) and leucine zipper kinase (LZK) as promising neuroprotective
targets in retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degenerations/optic neuropathies like glaucoma. More recently, we have used
chemical genetic and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-based screens in RGCs to identify
a set of sterile 20 (STE20) kinases that regulate DLK/LZK. In this proposal, we explore novel mechanisms by which STE20
kinases regulate this key neuronal injury pathway and exploit this knowledge to develop robust neuroprotective and
neuroregenerative strategies that we then test in rodent models of glaucoma.

title: Development of Novel PROTACs Targeting the ENL YEATS Domain for Treating MLL-rearranged Leukemias
text:
Pediatric leukemia patients bearing Mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL) gene translocations are associated with
dismal prognosis and poor response to standard treatments. This proposal aims to develop novel ENL small-
molecule degraders as in vivo chemical probes to target ENL, a promising drug target we recently identified, and
test our therapeutic hypothesis that pharmacological degradation of ENL will provide a novel and effective
strategy for treating MLL-rearranged leukemias. The proposed research is directly relevant to public health.

title: Decoding the metabolic routes of purine nucleotides in cancer - Resubmission - 1
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE ̶The proposed research is relevant to public health because it will advance our
understanding of how tumors acquire and regulate their nucleotide supply to support rapid cell growth.
Additionally, it will uncover how nucleotides obtained from our diet, particularly those rich in animal products,
affect tumor growth. Finally, our study has the potential to identify new avenues for targeting nucleotide supply
mechanisms in tumors, thereby eradicating cancer growth and resistance.

title: A Translational Bioinformatics Approach for Phenotyping and Genetic Risk of Severe Cutaneous Adverse Drug Reactions
text:
Severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions are life-threatening, associated with long-term morbidity, potentially
preventable, and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) restricted immune-mediated adverse drug reactions. Using a
translational bioinformatics approach, we will assemble one the largest cohorts of vancomycin-induced drug
reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) as a model to identify what comorbidities, genetic,
and other multi-omic risk factors interact with HLA to confer the resistance or susceptibility to DRESS. This
research will enable treating clinicians to better prevent, diagnose, and treat severe cutaneous adverse drug
reactions, bringing personalized care to patients.

title: Control of epithelial morphology and bioenergetics by Toll receptors during dynamic tissue remodeling
text:
Defects in epithelial morphology contribute to a wide range of human pathologies, including birth defects, cancer,
impaired wound healing, and inflammation, so therefore, a primary focus of developmental biology has been to
uncover the mechanisms that control epithelial cell shape. Studies of epithelial tissue elongation and wound
healing have shown that Toll family receptors and mitochondria are critical players in the regulation of tension
and adhesion at the cell membrane, although the molecular links between these processes are still being
uncovered. This proposal will address how signaling by Toll receptors and mitochondrial networks interact to
drive cell shape change during tissue elongation––revealing how biomechanics and bioenergetics are
coordinately regulated during embryonic development and shedding light on how these processes are
misregulated in disease states.

title: Harnessing Immune System to Target Adrenal Cancer Microenvironment
text:
Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a devastating cancer with a 35% 5-survival, and no effective chemotherapy
or targeted therapy are available for patients. In a recent retrospective study, we showed that some patients with
ACC might respond to combination of two therapies together, mitotane and an immunotherapy, pembrolizumab.
This proposal explores how mitotane changes the ACC tumors to improve the effectiveness of immunotherapy,
and we will use both human tumor tissue and ACC pre-clinical models to investigate this.

title: Single cell determinants of brain in the context of viral persistence in SIV/cART/cocaine non-human primates
text:
People living with HIV (PLWH) are at the higher risk for impaired cognitive functions due to higher use of
cocaine that could affect their immune functions and exacerbate CNS (central nervous system) impairment.
However, little is known about the HIV harboring cell types in brain, effect of therapy on specific CNS cell
types, and the modification of brain functions by cocaine use. Results of proposed innovative single-cell
studies employing simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) infection and nonhuman primate animal models will
generate cellular part list for brain regions and will illuminate novel insights into transcriptomic and epigenetic
landscapes of CNS and how they are altered by viral infections and cocaine use.

title: Defining the Scope and Consequences of Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis in Hospitalized Patients
text:
Gut microbiome dysbiosis has been linked to antimicrobial resistant (AR) infections and poor clinical outcomes
in multiple populations. However, these populations are highly select, accounting for only a fraction of at-risk
patients. To determine the scope and consequences of gut microbial dysbiosis among a large at-risk
population, Dr. Lehmann will characterize the microbiomes and metabolomes of general acute care hospital
patients establishing the prevalence of dysbiosis and AR pathogen expansion in the hospital setting.

title: Mechanisms of fasting-induced radioprotection of small intestinal epithelial cells
text:
Gastrointestinal toxicity often limits the amount of radiation that can be given to cancer patients. Our studies
will determine how fasting protects small intestinal epithelial cells from high dose radiation therapy (RT) with
the ultimate goal of mitigating deleterious side effects associated with RT so that dose escalation regimens can
be employed for efficient tumor cell killing.
